Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
become overly compliant when feeling threatened

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette: Arjun was nineteen when the road to the border became a corridor of smoke and shouting. He remembers the dust kicking up beneath the tires of the truck that carried his family, the sudden screech of brakes, and the way the soldiers in dark uniforms stepped out with rifles slung across their shoulders. When the engine stalled near an open stretch of desert, there was nowhere to hide. He watched men fall, their clothing tearing to reveal raw, bleeding skin, and heard the radio chatter about a recent collision on the supply route. His body had curled low behind a supply crate, breath held tight, counting the boots until the vehicles finally pulled away. He made it across, but his younger brother did not. Years later, the memory would not arrive as a story. It came as fragments: the smell of burnt rubber, the taste of copper, a sudden tightness in his chest. When he tried to speak of it, his throat would close, leaving him unable to form the words. Sometimes he could picture the checkpoint clearly, yet he felt no heat in his veins, as though he were watching a documentary about another man’s life. Other times, the stillness would break, and a wave of grief would knock him to his knees, heavy and suffocating. The fragments were pulled loose by everyday sounds. The wail of an ambulance on the street below his apartment made his hands freeze around a cutting board. When coworkers at the bistro talked excitedly about a pile-up on the interstate, Arjun would excuse himself, stepping into the walk-in cooler until his breathing steadied. He could not watch his line cooks clean a split knuckle or a gashed forearm; the sight of exposed tissue made his vision blur. He stopped walking past police cruisers parked outside the market, steering his footsteps toward the covered alleys instead. Working the dinner service at a downtown restaurant required a different kind of navigation. Before stepping onto the tiled floor, Arjun’s eyes would track the kitchen doors, the fire exit, the service stairs, mapping every possible path out before he felt safe enough to tie his apron. He moved through the dining room like a shadow, his attention darting to every raised voice, every sudden movement. He found himself unable to focus on the evening’s menu changes or the supplier invoices; his mind would snag on a flickering ceiling light or the scuff of a shoe against tile. When a regular customer raised his voice over a wrong order, Arjun would nod quickly, agree to remake the dish twice, and apologize for mistakes that were not his. The compliance and the hyperawareness filled his shifts side by side. He avoided the wide plaza behind the restaurant where the wind offered no cover, preferring the narrow service corridors where walls closed in on either side. The isolation accumulated quietly. He skipped family dinners, told dates he was busy, and let the silence of his apartment stretch into weeks. At work, the constant need to map exits and yield to every demand fractured his rhythm. He began leaving trays of food unattended at the pass, trusting his sous chef to step in, and missed a promotion that required leading the dinner shift. Arjun had come to believe he was permanently damaged, that the man who crossed that border had been stripped of something essential. He was certain he would never forgive himself for the choices he had not made, and he carried the weight of those who stayed behind in the dust. The tipping point came on a Tuesday when a food delivery driver backed his van into a lamppost outside the restaurant’s rear entrance. The driver was fine, but his neck hung at an unnatural angle, and the passenger door crumpled inward. Arjun had dropped a tray of garnishes, standing frozen until the manager’s hand on his shoulder finally pulled him back to the line. That night, he sat at his kitchen table, staring at the stillness between his hands, and realized he could no longer pretend the fear was a phase. He made an appointment with a therapist, hoping someone might help him unclench his shoulders and teach him how to live inside his own body again. What frightened him most was that the past might always be waiting in the next siren, the next crash, the next exposed stretch of road, and that he would never be allowed to stay still.
